object_entity.notes: Head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; author of Protrepticus, Paedagogus, and Stromateis; synthesized Christian faith with Greek philosophy; key witness for Alexandrian baptismal theology, eucharistic practice, asceticism, and apostolic tradition.

evidence.notes: This passage from the work attests its existence and authorship.

passage.excerpt: The New Song has sprung up, eternal, which has also become new for the new people — the Lord himself, who, being a new light above the sun, has risen upon those living in darkness and the shadow of death. Behold the might of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts. Those who were as dead, not being partakers of the true life, have come to life again, simply by becoming listeners to this song.
passage.notes: Christ as the divine new song; pre-existent Logos incarnate calling all to life and salvation

subject_entity.notes: Tertullian's treatise c. 200 arguing that heretics have no right to appeal to Scripture; the Church alone possesses the apostolic tradition and succession that guarantees correct interpretation.

object_entity.notes: First major Latin Christian author; active in Carthage c. 195–220. Wrote at least 31 works spanning apologetics, anti-heretical polemic, and moral discipline. Coined 'trinitas' and 'tres personae una substantia'. Defender of apostolic succession, rule of faith, incarnation, and bodily resurrection. Later attracted to Montanist rigorism c. 207; teacher of Cyprian by doctrinal influence.

passage.excerpt: The rule of faith is altogether one, alone immovable and irreformable: to believe in one God omnipotent, maker of the world; and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, on the third day raised from the dead, received in the heavens, sitting now at the right hand of the Father, and coming to judge the living and the dead through the resurrection of the flesh.
passage.notes: The rule of faith stated; creedal summary; apostolic tradition; irreformable confession

passage.excerpt: Come now, you who wish to exercise your curiosity, run over the apostolic churches, in which the very seats of the apostles still preside at their own places; in which their authentic letters are read. Achaia is close to you — you have Corinth. If you are not far from Macedonia — you have Philippi, you have the Thessalonians. If you can go to Asia — you have Ephesus. But if you are near to Italy — you have Rome, whence our own authority derives also.
passage.notes: Apostolic sees as living witnesses to the faith; Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Ephesus named; authority of apostolic churches

object_entity.proposition_label: The succession of bishops in their see guarantees the apostolic faith
object_entity.description: The see of the bishop, transmitted through orderly succession, is the locus and guarantee of the faith received from the apostles.

context_place.notes: Major North African city; center of Latin Christianity from Tertullian through Cyprian and Augustine; seat of important regional councils.

evidence.notes: Apostolic churches transmit tradition through founding lineage

passage.excerpt: The apostles first bore witness to the faith in Christ Jesus throughout Judaea and founded churches there; then went out into the world and preached the same doctrine of the same faith to the nations. They likewise founded churches in every city, from which the other churches borrowed the tradition of the faith and the seeds of doctrine, and are every day borrowing them to become churches. And therefore these churches are counted apostolic, being the offspring of apostolic churches. Every kind of thing must be classed according to its origin. These churches then are apostolic, in that they are derived from apostolic churches.
passage.notes: Apostolic succession of churches; tradition transmitted through founding churches; seed metaphor

subject_entity.notes: Hippolytus's commentary on Daniel c. 204; the earliest known patristic biblical commentary to survive in substantial form; contains the earliest reference to Christ's birth being celebrated on December 25; interprets Daniel's prophecies christologically; opposes imminent eschatological expectations.

object_entity.notes: Roman presbyter and theologian; prolific Greek-speaking writer in Rome; opposed the modalism of Zephyrinus and Callistus; set himself up as rival bishop c. 217 (sometimes called the first antipope); exiled with Pontian to Sardinia in 235; reconciled before death; author of the Apostolic Tradition, Refutation of All Heresies, Against Noetus, and Commentary on Daniel.

evidence.notes: Commentary on Daniel is securely attributed to Hippolytus by scholarly consensus.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: The first advent of our Lord in the flesh took place in Bethlehem, under Augustus, in the year 5500 from Adam. He suffered in his thirty-third year. And six thousand years must be completed before the second coming, so five hundred years still remain.
passage.notes: Earliest reference to Christ's birth being celebrated on December 25; eschatological chronology; opposes imminentism
